that at least the requirement that those two things add up to 85 would be reduced to 80 or 75 or even 70.
Even though the hon. member for Kent-Essex can argue that there has been some parallelism produced in that the same rule applies to members of the armed forces as applies to senior public servants, it is the old story of one horse and one rabbit, or the rich and poor both having the right to sleep under the bridge. There is such a difference in the terms of employment that it does not turn out to be as equal as the hon. member suggests. Therefore I think what is asked for in this motion should receive favourable and active consideration.
I believe that the members of the Canadian Armed Forces Long Service Pensioners Association are to be complimented on saying that they will settle for something less than they originally requested. Originally their request was that escalation begin the year following retirement, no matter what the age, but they are taking the position now that at least a formula which adds up to something below 85-80, 75 or 70, which was what was discussed when the committee dealt with this in December of 1976-is a responsible and reasonable proposal.
Because we are in private members' hour when time is of the essence, I must not carry on. I saw two or three others wanting to get to their feet. I hope they will all be on the same side and that they will be brief. Escalation of pensions is a good idea, and the thing to do by way of resolving the issue out in the country these days is not to take it away from those who have it but to see that it is extended to everyone, and that being the case I think we should take this step of improving the escalation of the pensions of those in the armed forces and in the RCMP.
I was glad to note the reference several times by the last speaker to the fact that this is a shared cost proposition and that the money which goes into the fund out of which escalation is paid is contributed 50-50 by the employees and the government. I would just like to emphasize that the government in that case is making that payment as an employer, not as the government, which I suggest makes quite a difference.
Sir, I stand, as I have for these many years, a strong supporter of the idea that people in retirement should have their incomes maintained at a level which enables them to keep up with the cost of living, or better still, to keep up with the standard of living, and I think we owe this to those in the RCMP and the Canadian Armed Forces whom we call on to retire early. Therefore, I am in full support of the motion which is now before the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian Armed Forces pensioners are protesting waits of up to 15 years for their first pension payments. Under the current system, forces employees must retire in their forties if they have served 20 to 25 years.
Eligibility for pension payment is decided in the same way as in the public service. Retired persons must wait until their age plus their years of service equal an arbitrarily chosen figure of 85. Canada's 50,000 retired servicemen want that

arbitrary figure lowered to 70 so retired personnel can use the retirement fund when it is most needed, soon after leaving the forces. Retired servicemen must often take lower paying jobs after leaving the forces in early middle age, at a time when their children often are about to enter university.
Mr. Frank McNeil, the national director of the Canadian Forces Long Service Pensioners Association, has stated that each year $130 million is paid in forces pensions, that lowering the age of eligibility for pension payments would cost an additional $8 million per year, and that this could be taken from the $210 million earned annually by the fund in interest. It would not cost taxpayers a cent, so I fully and wholeheartedly support the motion moved by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker), which is as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of amending the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act to provide for the reduction of the "Magic 85" formula to 70 and the indexing of the new formula to the cost of living.
I suggest that we close the debate at this time, let this motion be considered by the government, and that the government take immediate action to change the formula from 85 to 70.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak for a few minutes on this motion. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) for bringing it forward.
I represent a large number of military people, many of whom have reached pensionable age and some of whom have been retired for varying lengths of time. Some have made representations to me on the very point the hon. member opposite raises. I would guess that most members of the House are supportive of doing this when it can be afforded and at the time that the survey which is under way is in and analyzed. Certainly my first step was to try to understand the rather complex question of pensions as they apply to employees of the Department of National Defence as well as to public servants. The pensions are calculated on a quite complex formula. I spent some time reviewing the situation and I should like to offer a few comments on it.
As a general rule when I speak in the House I use only limited notes, but in this case, like the hon. member who proposed the motion, I should like to follow my notes very carefully. Even after investigating this quite thoroughly I find it a rather complex subject which requires a great deal of attention to detail.
My colleague, the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Dau-dlin), has gone over the background of the present indexing arrangements very extensively and has outlined the format for members of the Canadian forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, that is, the so-called "85 formula". The formula is now calculated with reference to the consumer price index.
June 6, 1977

Pension Index 1976
The pension index for a given year is equal to the average of the consumer price index over the period from October to September of the previous year. For example, the pension index for 1977 equals the average of the consumer price index from October, 1975, to September, 1976.
The total increase paid over and above an individual's basic pension in a given year is determined by the ratio of the benefit index for that year to the benefit index for his/her year of retirement. For example, the increase payable in 1977 to a person retired in 1972 equals the basic pension multiplied by the benefit index for 1977 divided by the benefit index for 1972.
When the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act was introduced in 1970, the benefit index was set at 100 for that year and the benefit indices for previous years back to 1952 were determined accordingly. At that time the benefit indices for subsequent years could not be more than 2 per cent greater than the benefit index of the previous year. However, effective January, 1974, this ceiling was removed. The benefit indices for the years 1971, 1972 and 1973 were re-calculated to take this change into account, so that in 1974 persons who retired in 1973 or earlier received a pension increase in line with the rise in the consumer price index since their year of retirement.
The benefit index for 1977 is, I understand, 158.02, so that, for example, in 1977, a person who retired in 1970 when the benefit index was 100, would receive an increase of 58 per cent.
In the fashion I have outlined above, then pensions payable under legislation to which the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act applies are already escalated to equal the increase in the cost of living. The motion under discussion would therefore only have the effect of applying full indexing of the pensions of former members of the armed forces, Royal Canadian Mount-

I do not propose to go over all of the arguments pro and con that have been raised in connection with this issue, or indeed many that I have researched myself. I would, however, like to speak about the Financial implications of an extension of the pension increases payable under the present legislation.
One needs only to look at the annual reports on the administration of the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act since 1970 to see that the amounts involved in paying for full pension escalation are sizeable. For example, in the three fiscal years since full indexing was introduced, the pension increases payable under the act have been as follows: 1974-75= $58,878,000;	1975-76=590,768,000;	1976-77=$131,000,000
approximately.
I am sure other members of the House have had representations from many constituents and organizations about the level of government spending. While we all support this motion I do not think the financial implications can be totally overlooked when related to government expenditure of that magnitude.
Although I do not have any over-all estimates of the cost implications of the proposal before us at this time, I can present a single example of the cost involved in this motion. Let us take the case of the 45-year old serviceman with 25 years' service who retires on a $7,000 pension. If we assume a 5 per cent rate of inflation between his year of retirement and the year he reaches age 60, the granting of a full indexing immediately would mean additional payments between ages 45 and 60 of about $46,000, or 6.57 times the basic pension.
As illustrated then, the potential cost of instituting the proposed change would be significant. A further indication of the cost of pension escalation can readily be seen if one refers to the last page of the "Basic Facts" paper tabled by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) on October 18, 1976. That page outlines the projected cost of the public service plan, and it can be seen that based on certain economic assumptions the cost of pension escalation will eventually equal the cost of the basic plan itself.
In drawing these points to the attention of the House I would not want it to be construed that I think most members do not support the intent of the motion, but I think it is fair to ask that we look at the cost as well. I am sure all members

June 6, 1977
Retirement Benefits
agree that the whole question of pensions has become an issue in the past year. Many people write to us with a point of view that is perhaps not based totally on fact regarding public service pensions and pensions for members of the armed forces.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made a valid point when he said we should consider this subject objectively. He suggested that before anyone says that current pension benefits should be reduced we should review pension benefits made available to the public service and armed services. Indeed most people from my riding who have written to me about the cost of indexing seem worried about the open ended nature of these commitments. They fear that future costs may be so high as to create financial difficulties for the federal treasury, and pension benefits could be much higher than those the private sector could provide. Surely there should be some relationship between pension plans which can and should be provided by the private sector and the public sector.
The coupling of indexing with the early retirement provisions of the public service plan, not to mention the even earlier retirement provisions of the armed forces and Royal Canadian Mounted Police plans, has led to widespread criticism being levelled against the pension plans of federal employees, to the effect that "fat" and "exorbitant" pensions generally place those employees in a privileged position relative to other Canadians, at the expense of taxpayers. I was glad to see that in response to these criticisms the President of the Treasury Board prepared certain information.
I was one of the members who asked the minister to compile certain factual information on pension plans and made it available to all members of parliament so that we could render some mature judgment on the validity of the charges which had been made, instead of agreeing or disagreeing without information to temper our judgment.
I think the paper "Basic Facts" concerning pension plans helped to set the record straight. Though that paper was tabled, the debate on the question of pensions has continued and various groups in the community have levelled charges and made counter charges. As the paper pointed out, federal public servants have made consistently high employee contributions over the years. I think hon. members ought to remember this and comment on it more often. The plan was begun many years ago and the paper emphasized the actuarial soundness of the plan. That document also commented on a number of developments which would give the government the opportunity to reassess public service pension plan benefits and financial provisions in the near future. While referring specifically to the pension plan for public servants, needless to say any reassessment would also involve the pension plan for members of the armed forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The first development concerns the current work in progress within the Treasury Board secretariat to establish a compre-

hensive framework within which the total compensation paid to federal employees can be measured with greater accuracy and related more systematically to total compensation rates in other sectors of the economy. This is important. I certainly do not support the argument that public servants should be paid less than their counterparts in the private sector. Surely the same responsibilities should be rewarded with the same pay, no matter if the work is done in the public or private sector. The new framework is designed to facilitate Treasury Board's continuing efforts to ensure that all elements of compensation for federal employees, including pension entitlement, are maintained in an equitable relationship with compensation levels in comparable areas of the private and public sectors.
A second development will be the next actuarial valuations of the public service, armed forces and Mounted Police pension plans scheduled to be conducted over the next two years. These valuations will assess, among other things, the financial impact on pension accounts and the implications for the future of the recent experience of high inflation. This is a key point, because our high inflation rates have made people concerned about the indexing cost of pensions. They would also provide the government with reliable information on which to base a reconsideration of any aspects of its pension policies for its employees which may be required. Indeed, I hope we shall have an opportunity to debate these questions in the House and to make representations to the governement on this issue which is of interest to many Canadians.
A third development concerns the government's general study of the pension situation of all Canadians. As reported last fall by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), officials of the Departments of National Health and Welfare, Finance and Insurance, with the co-operation of interested federal departments and agencies, including the Treasury Board secretariat, have been laying the technical groundwork for this study by carrying out basic research, studying and analysing statistical and other information, and assembling the suggestions and comments of interested individuals and organizations. The review, I understand, will include comparisons of the features of retirement plans in the private and public sectors.
As the President of the Treasury Board mentioned, the government is well aware that pension policy for the public service cannot be considered in isolation from the pension situation of other Canadians, or without reference to the needs and capacities of other sectors of the economy. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre raised a good point when he said that the result of this may be a review of where the private sector stands in providing adequate pensions to its employees. That question may be even more important than the analysis of pensions in the public sector.
A further major development was the announcement on March 14 this year by the President of the Treasury Board in an address to the Canadian Pension Conference, a reading of which I commend to hon. members, of the appointment of an outside consulting firm to conduct an independent study of the
June 6, 1977

public service pension program. In announcing the study the minister mentioned a number of questions about pensions which had been brought to his attention. They were: what are the net costs associated with indexing pensions to the cost of living? Do they vary between the federal public sector and the private sector and, if so, why? Second, what roles have interest earnings and other pension investment returns played in the financing of pensions in the public and private sectors? Do these roles vary and, if so, why; and what are the implications of these variations?

SUPPLY AND SERVICES-REASON FOR FAILURE OF DEPARTMENT TO MAKE A FAIR PERCENTAGE OF PURCHASES IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to return to the matter I raised on May 26 with the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer). As I understand it, the minister is out of the country at the moment. I believe he is in Africa. That will give him time to reflect on the answer he gave the other day. I regard this a very serious matter, as I am sure whoever will be responding for the government also does.
It came to my attention a couple of weeks ago that, along with other aspects of federal policy which may be continuing or exacerbating regional disparity, particularly in the Atlantic region, the purchasing or procurement policies of the Department of Supply and Services seemed to have particular significance. I raise this because recently we received figures on two aspects of the Department of Supply and Services, their procurement policy with respect to science and engineering, and with regard to commercial supply.
With regard to commercial supply in 1976-1977, the year that has just concluded, there was a purchasing power of 6.3 per cent from a total budget of $1,009,486,000. This 6.3 per cent represented purchases made in the Atlantic region. That was a reduction from 7.9 per cent in the previous year,
1975-	76, both in terms of over-all expenditures and absolute reduction $66,584,000 to something like $64,227,000 in 197677. That is a serious decline from 7.9 per cent to 6.3 per cent when you realize that the population in the Atlantic provinces is roughly 9.5 per cent of the national population.
When you look at the other area, that of science and engineering, the total is much larger, $1,862,722,000. We discover there is a shocking situation. There has been a decline because of the increase in the budget in that area in proportionate terms from 4.1 per cent in 1975-76 to 2 per cent in
1976-	77, and an absolute decline from $41,305,000 to $37,563,000.
When you look at the fact that only 2 per cent of purchasing under science and engineering is directed to the Atlantic
6346

June 6, 1977
Adjournment Debate
provinces you realize that we are in a very serious situation. On a proportionate basis the Atlantic provinces are not receiving their fair share of federal contracts through the Department of Supply and Services.
More important, the direction with respect to purchasing seems to be creating greater hardship and reducing, both on an absolute basis and in absolute terms, the amount of money expended in the Atlantic provinces, this at a time when we have the highest unemployment ever in the Atlantic provinces.
I was shocked by this revelation. Added to that shock was the answer I received from the Minister of Supply and Services. He said that his department was not responsible for the industrial base within the various regions of our country. Further, in response to my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco), the minister said that "it was a matter of not indulging in discriminatory policies towards any area, but rather to help businessmen in remote areas of the country to do business with us".
It seems that the minister is virtually unaware both of the impact of his department's billion dollar expenditures in terms of exacerbating the problems of regional economies across the country and, equally serious, he is not aware of even the Prime Minister's own dictum and instruction, because in reply to a supplementary from me the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said he could assure me that it was made a matter of policy some years ago that, so far as possible, the department would ensure that regional considerations and the concern for greater equalization were taken into account in the purchasing done by the department.
Where is the recognition on the part of the minister? I know he has difficulty sometimes facing up to reality. He admitted as much in his terse note before he left the country in regard to another incident which I will not refer to in this question period. If the Prime Minister has issued to the minister- indeed, to all members of the cabinet-the instruction that he has a basic responsibility with respect to the impact on regional economies of a department which enters into billions of dollars worth of contracts, why does he say his department is not responsible, that this policy does not take any cognizance whatever of regional variations in the country? In fact he says it is not a matter of indulging in discriminatory policies.
Would the minister suggest that the recent innovation by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in his latest budget in regard to the variable tax rate, which rises to 10 per cent for the Atlantic provinces, is a form of this regional discrimination in which the government should not engage? Would he suggest with respect to the attempt to vary freight rates across the country in order to make various producers equally competitive that this is a form of discrimination in which the government should not engage? Would he suggest that the millions of dollars worth of tariffs which have been imposed over the years is a form of discrimination which should not be pursued?
Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I think all members of the House recognize the fact that the federal government has a responsibility to ensure, as much as possible, that it takes overt and effective action to offset the various regional problems

which we in this country face. For the minister to accept no responsibility and to ignore the declining interest in this department-in fact an overt attack on a regional economy such as that in the Atlantic provinces-through a declining budget commitment, is simply unacceptable. I hope that the minister or his parliamentary secretary will give us some effective answer and some redress on this matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mike Landers (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: SUPPLY AND SERVICES-REASON FOR FAILURE OF DEPARTMENT TO MAKE A FAIR PERCENTAGE OF PURCHASES IN ATLANTIC REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to respond to questions posed on May 26 by the hon. members for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) and Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) concerning the distribution of DSS contracts in Atlantic and western Canada.
First, I would like to point out that it is not the government's policy to allocate contracts for federal government requirements on the basis of the distribution of the Canadian population. Such a policy would be neither reasonable nor practical, as it is based on the assumption that the structure of economic activity is the same throughout the country. Our aim, as indicated by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) on May 26, is to ensure that all Canadian businessmen who wish to do so have an equal opportunity to compete for federal government contracts. The minister has already described the work being done to inform suppliers of how to do business with government in order to increase the volume of contracts going into the industrial base in both the Atlantic and Pacific regions.
Within the government's over-all policy of competitive bidding, it is DSS's policy to employ a regional preference policy for local requirements where possible and practical. That is to say, we purchase federal government needs for goods from sources of supply close to the point of use when reasonable competition can be obtained among local suppliers. This policy, plus the general practice of acquiring goods and services on a competitive basis, has resulted in a considerable number of contracts being placed in Atlantic and western Canada. In fact our analysis shows that the federal government buys substantially more in Atlantic and western Canada than it consumes in those areas.
The hon. member has noted a sharp decline year over year in certain of our regional statistics. He will understand that a substantial part of our business relates to the acquisition of large value capital equipment which is bought infrequently. Consequently the value of business placed can fluctuate widely from one year to the next. A case in point would be the "R" class icebreaker which was contracted for in British Columbia last year. This one contract amounted to $108 million. Naturally the annual contracting values will decrease significantly in the year following such an acquisition.
I am sure hon. members will recognize that the total benefits accruing to any given region are not reflected in DSS's own contracting statistics. For example, the foreign prime contractors for large equipment purchases for the Department of National Defence are required to place business in Canada, as a result of contract conditions negotiated by DSS. Two
June 6, 1977

contracts were recently placed as a result of such arrangements with firms in Amherst and Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, for requirements potentially totalling $13.5 million.
We share hon. members' concern about increasing the amount of contracting done in Atlantic and western Canada. We intend to continue to work to increase this level of business, while continuing to recognize our over-all responsibility to spend the taxpayers' money in a judicious, fair, and reasonable manner. Members must, however, realize, as we now do, the real constraints we face in achieving this objective. The Department of Supply and Services buys a large amount of goods and related services. However, the economies of the west and the Atlantic region do not always produce the type of goods we are asked to buy. In a few cases we may be able to integrate our purchasing with the industrial development plans of the regions. In most cases, however, we will have to continue to rely on existing facilities to meet our needs.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-REASON FOR FAILURE TO PURSUE CASE AGAINST JOHN DOYLE UNDER INCOME TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 4 I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) a question about a case of gross negligence, wanton and wilful misconduct in the administration of the laws of this country, which had to do with the Department of National Revenue. It was a situation where a taxpayer, one John C. Doyle, was re-assessed for taxes in 1950 and 1954. It was 27 years ago in one case, and 24 years ago in the other. They were eventually brought before the Income Tax Appeal Board and were lost there. They were appealled to the Exchequer Court of Canada and lost there in 1970. There was another appeal entered in October, 1970, and these two cases are still unheard as I speak in this Chamber now.
On February 8 I tabled a question here about the same matter, and it is still unanswered. I wrote the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) and the Minister of Justice on March 23, and I got no response from them. I finally spoke in the House on this matter on April 21. On April 22, I wrote to both ministers and sent them a copy of my speech. I still have had no response from them. I asked the question again on May 4 in the House, and I spoke on May 5 in the House concerning this.
The Minister of Justice has made some extraordinary excuses. In answer to my question on May 4 he said that these appeals were proceeding at a pace the rules of the court allowed, and seemed to suggest that it was somehow the fault of the Supreme Court of Canada that this matter had not been concluded; whereas it is the negligence of the Department of Justice and the Department of National Revenue which permitted this thing to drag on as it has.
In the debate on the Judges Act on May 5, the Minister of Justice suggested that I should accept his statements, that there was no negligence on the part of the minister or his officials in this 27 year fiasco. Having said that once, he expected me to accept his statement instead of challenging it.
Adjournment Debate
That is a new principle of parliamentary immunity, Mr. Speaker, that if a minister says there has been no negligence on the part of a minister or any of his officials, that must be accepted and no one dare challenge that statement. Of course that is quite untrue.
If the minister says he is now instructing his officials to proceed with all deliberate speed and haste to have the appeals heard, I would accept his word; but when he says there has been no negligence, I do not accept that statement. In my opinion there has been gross negligence and misconduct in this matter for the last 27 years. How could appeals involving millions of dollars in public funds be left to lie fallow for several years without any action by the department, not to mention the fact that the department consented when the appellant asked for the matter to be postponed last year?
I have still no answer to my question of February 8, although the minister wrote me on May 13, gave me the information and said it would soon be tabled. It has not been tabled as yet. I do not know what is happening. I do not know whether someone is preventing this information from being tabled.

COMMONWEALTH GAMES-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO AVOID AFRICAN BOYCOTT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for many months I have been urging the government to take every step possible to ensure the success of the Commonwealth Games in Edmonton in 1978. We are all worried about national unity today. I can tell you what would be a magnificent boost for unity-both in Canada and the Commonwealth-and that would be the complete participation by every Commonwealth nation. In other words, no African boycott.
The fact that the possibility of an African boycott is on the agenda of the Commonwealth conference next week is proof that the Canadian government has so far failed to resolve this matter. And the government has failed because it has not exerted enough muscle. It has been too timid. It has not been tough enough with either New Zealand or the African states.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the problem revolves around New Zealand's sporting links with South Africa. In the view of the black African states it is not good enough for New Zealand to have severed official sporting links with South Africa because of its apartheid policies. The black states want New Zealand to ban teams even from unofficial sports contests in South Africa.
For its part, New Zealand's Prime Minister, Mr. Muldoon, said recently that the Commonwealth Games are "not sufficiently important" for New Zealand to stop its teams. That was when the Canadian government should have made it abundantly clear that it would not tolerate such a cavalier attitude by a sister country. The games are an essential instrument in the development of relations between every member of the Commonwealth. The government took this snubbing by New Zealand because it did not have the courage to fight for our rights. It relied on the customary mode of quiet diplomacy when it should have acted to urge New Zealand to wake up.
June 6, 1977

Similarly what is the Canadian government doing to put some pressure on the African nations? What right do they have to penalize Canada because of the obfuscations of New Zealand? Canada's record on race relations is one we can be and are proud of. This country has helped black African nations politically and economically to attain their independence and maturity.
And speaking of economic help, how can the African states call for Canada's help in improving the health of developing nations through such instruments as the just-concluded North-South Conference in Paris if, at the same time, they hurt us economically?
It is time the African nations also woke up and realized that we live in an interdependent world. Pulling out of the 1978 games and hurting Canada is not a very good way to develop public opinion in Canada concerning the needs of the developing countries.
So, Mr. Speaker, there are a lot of hard-headed attitudes at the root of the Commonwealth Games problem. And the Canadian government has taken too soft a stand.
Edmonton has done a superlative job in preparing the facilities, which are acknowledged to be the finest ever built for the Commonwealth Games. Good management by the Edmonton organizers has kept the planning on budget and ahead of schedule.
The total cost of this great effort is under $50 million, including capital and operating costs, a truly remarkable achievement when we consider $1,416 billion spent on the 1976 Montreal Olympics. We are preparing for 24,000 visitors from around the world who will be in Edmonton for each of the ten days, August 3-12, 1978. They will all receive a royal welcome. The members of the news media will total more than 1,300.
All of this is more than just a great community effort of 3,000 volunteers brought together by a great Edmonton team headed by Dr. Maury Van Vliet. It is a vital national event, and it cannot be allowed to fail or be crippled by an African boycott.
I want a response from the government tonight that will tell me more than just the amount of federal money contributed. I want to know how a boycott can be avoided, since efforts have so far failed. The Commonwealth conference appears to be the last hope. If that conference is not successful, Canada ought to bring the issue to the United Nations, for the issue is not the politics of sports; the issue is the development of good relations in a global community. That is an issue for all nations and all colours of people, and Canada can no longer remain silent.

Mr. Speaker, the question which the hon. member has raised is a very difficult one which has concerned the government for many months. The government is committed to the success of the Commonwealth Games in Edmonton, both as a sporting event and as a symbol of what the Commonwealth means as a harmonious association of peoples. We are, therefore, concerned that there
Fishing and Recreational Harbours be representation from all parts of the Commonwealth; indeed we are concerned that lack of such representation would be a severe blow to the fabric of the Commonwealth.
We have been working closely with the Secretary General of the Commonwealth and with other Commonwealth countries to bring about a successful resolution of the points at issue between New Zealand and the African members of the Commonwealth. We believe there is a good chance that the issue can be settled at the heads of government meeting in London, and we are working to set the stage for a constructive discussion of the issue at that time. We believe that it is possible for a compromise to be achieved on the basis of the opposition of all Commonwealth members to the system of apartheid.
What we envisage is a statement by all heads of government reaffirming their opposition to the practice of apartheid in sport and to contacts with South Africa by Commonwealth sports bodies and individuals. The Secretary General has been charged with finding a suitable formula for discussion, and the exact content of the statement will no doubt be a matter for debate among heads of government.

Mr. Speaker, I understand of course that the hon. member is interested in this problem since he comes from a constituency in Edmonton, but he should understand that in three minutes it is impossible to give the answers to all the points that this very complex problem might raise and I am sorry not to be able to give him a more complete answer, but the discussions are still going on and it would be presumptuous to give more complete answers at this moment.

Mr. Speaker, I earlier mentioned my concern about wharfage. In the interim I have had an opportunity to look into the subject a little deeper, and there are some matters I should like to put on the record.
The first is an exchange between myself and the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) which took place at the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry on May 30, 1975, when I put the following question:
... let us resolve this wharfage business. Let us wipe it out and start over ...
And the minister replied:
I will say amen to that.
Every member present at that committee meeting was under the impression that the minister had given his approval to the principle of eliminating wharfage as a fee against fishermen and other boat owners.
On May 27, 1975, a group of fishermen from the Fundy coast of New Brunswick appeared before the committee and the subject of wharfage came up again. I questioned Mr. Andrew Matthews, who was appearing for the second time, as follows:

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the new act which we hope to introduce very shortly, we have examined this whole area of user charges and the wharfinger system. We hope to be able to introduce a system of fees whereby a fisherman, or even the recreational boating public using federal facilities, will pay one fee a year which will give them the opportunity to dock at federal government facilities, so that it will no longer be the duty of the wharfinger to collect the fees from people as they are docking at federal government facilities.
Perhaps it would be wrong of me to ask if the Minister of Fisheries has any idea of the number of boats that go in and out of certain of those small craft facilities in a day, or a week, or even a season.
Is the government prepared to pay to the person responsible for collecting wharfage a proper amount of money, and so induce him to exercise surveillance over the port or harbour throughout the year, in order to assure its equitable use? Or, is it the government's policy to continue the patronage system, of

appointing friends to collect money from those from whom they wish to collect? I raise one more question.
The question I placed on the order paper on November 17 asked if there is a standard wharfage structure in eastern Canada. I was always under the impression eastern Canada included the five eastern provinces, in all of which there are opportunities for fishing and fish industries. If there is a wharfage structure in the province of Quebec, it is not listed in the answer. If fees were collected, they were not listed. If there is a charge system in the Quebec area of eastern Canada, that is not listed. I presume all this may be due to an oversight. But if it was not an oversight, I want the government to explain why my question was not answered adequately.
In the main, the present wharfage system is obnoxious and improperly managed. I see no indication in this bill that this will change. Apparently it will be perpetuated. That will be a perpetuation of wrong-doing.
Virtually the longest clause of Bill C-7 deals with the government's regulation making powers. It permits the government to make regulations with respect to the classification of harbours, payment of wharfage fees, penalties, and pollution. Subparagraph (d) of Clause 9 says that the Governor in Council may make regulations "not inconsistent with any other act of parliament or regulations made thereunder, for the control of pollution at any scheduled harbour."
There are already three acts in place on the statute books concerning small harbour facilities. Now a fourth statute is to be added. That this bill does not specify more clearly the minister's responsibility concerning non-fishing boats, pleasure craft and other boats is improper. It gives the harbour authorities no authority to reserve particular fishing facility for fishing boats. It will not resolve fishermen's complaints that pleasure craft using a harbour interfere with the fishermen's use of the harbour.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise this evening to discuss Bill C-7 respecting the administration and development of certain fishing and recreational harbours in Canada. I do not intend to linger on that legislation, except to say that it is somewhat late this year. Indeed, it
June 6, 1977

will no doubt be difficult if not impossible to benefit from this legislation this year, because the summer season has already begun. In spite of that fact, I must say that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) will give rise to many hopes with that bill, since it will enable individuals and corporations to take advantage of the financial and technical assistance of the department.
In my constituency, Marina regionale de Rimouski Inc. have been trying for several years to obtain assistance to build a marina in the port of Rimouski on a location recognized as being propitious to such an operation while not hindering any traffic of heavy tonnage. Environment Canada did receive a report from that organization requesting financial assistance to carry out its project. It now has 90 members waiting for the assistance of the federal department in this project.
Rimouski has a strategic position: it is located on the south shore of the St. Lawrence, 180 miles east of Quebec City and 345 miles northeast of Montreal. The average width of the river within the quadrilateral formed by Rivifire-du-Loup and Matane on the south shore and Godbout and Tadoussac on the north shore, of which Rimouski is the centre on the south shore, is about 30 to 40 miles. With the variety of services it provides, Rimouski could easily become the main centre for sailing and recreational activities in the eastern part of Quebec, an important halt for tourists coming from the Saguenay area, Quebec City, Montreal, the Richelieu Valley and the United States, and an open gate on ocean navigation for travellers heading for the Gaspe Peninsula, Anticosti Island and the Magdalen Islands. Rimouski is proud of the stretch of water it offers and conscious of its exceptional position as we can see by the number of boat owners, maritime and nautical sport clubs as well as the number of oceanologic institutions it harbours.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out in passing all the bodies interested in the development of Rimouski harbour. The town of Rimouski has its own school of maritime navigation affiliated with the college course of the education department. It also owns an oceanographic research centre affiliated with the University of Quebec at Rimouski; the group GIROQ, a provincial body for oceanographic research; a squadron of the Canadian Power Squadrons made up of 40 members, which for several years has been giving courses in maritime navigation and nautical safety; a sailing club of 125 members whose aim is to promote sailing and teach its technique. The sailing club is also greatly responsible for the only off-shore sailing regatta in the province of Quebec; this regatta is supported by the Federation de la voile du Quebec and the winner is awarded the Lieutenant-Governor's trophy. Rimouski also has a 100-member scuba-diving club and 10 boats from 20 to 45 feet long, a nautical club with 300 members and 100 yachts 12 to 20 feet long.
Mr. Speaker, 1 do not know if you are aware of that, but a few years ago, the highway department built a road that stretches about three miles along the shore of the St. Lawrence
Fishing and Recreational Harbours River. A retaining wall was also erected. Unfortunately that wall has the effect of breaking the waves which now causes a lot of damage to pleasure boats and even bigger ships during storms. I would also like to mention damages caused in recent years since the construction of the retaining wall. Damages have been caused to boats and their owners since 1972, the year when the retaining wall of Highway 132 was built. This list is not exhaustive and is only given to indicate the urgency of the situation: a 30-foot whaler sank; a visitor boat from the United States a 35-foot sloop, and a 40-foot school-ship from Montreal were damaged. More than twenty ships of all sizes, local and visitor, suffered various damages.
The summer of 1974 was particularly fertile in unfortunate events: one wrist fractured, one rudder broken, two stem galleries wrung, one chain plate torn off with part of the deck, one stay tightener twisted and one mast broken in three parts. Unfortunately, to this list we should add long hours of watching, smashed fences, gunwale rails ripped off and countless damages to fibre-glass hulls or painted surfaces.
Mr. Speaker, for all those reasons and many more to which we will come back during another debate, we believe it is at least abnormal if not unjust that Rimouski could not benefit from the necessary facilities to protect small crafts and visiting boats. Rimouski residents can only offer the federal harbour in Rimouski East to local sportsmen for the protection of their craft. Moreover, this relative security is granted to them only through simple and gracious permission of port authorities and it can be removed at any time because it is not part of a contractual negotiation as such. Although partial, the protection owners enjoyed before was acceptable. As I said earlier, the construction of a retaining wall is required for Highway 132 in front of the Rimouski-East wharf, and it has transformed this relative security into a real danger. This retaining wall is in fact dangerous and bounces the waves formed by the north and northeast winds directly back into the harbour where the boats are berthed. Those waves, with the Bernouilli phenomenon caused by the bottleneck shape of the wharf, are quite amplified and cause really disastrous and highly dangerous situations, especially since the foreign visitor, knowing nothing of the above mentioned phenomenon, is deluded by the apparent security of this haven.
This situation is not extraordinary, as it could be easily believed, and it is not necessarily accompanying unusually bad weather. Every time the wind blows from the north-northeast or east, and that the tide is rising, the worst can be expected and the worst usually happens. When referring to serious works in meteorology for the Rimouski area concerning prevalent winds for normal navigation, and reading in regard the data of the 1975 tide tables, if we synthetize those parameters even summarily, there is no point in mentioning the apprehension felt by vacationers concerning the opening of the next navigation season. If we add to all this the narrowness of this harbour where over 39 local boats were berthing last year, most of them in double, this year there will be some 15 additional boats. The situation is not only dangerous but catastrophic and it becomes intolerable.

June 6, 1977
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
As long as the present harbour is not extended and protected by at least one north-south breakwater on the east side, it will remain illusory to develop navigational tourism on the St. Lawrence and farther east all around the Gaspe Peninsula. As long as visitors will not be protected, it will always be a bit ridiculous to organize, at the regional level, off-shore boat races which would supposedly be of international levels. Yet it is the status which can be expected for the lieutenant-governor classic. The success met by this competition in the last few years as to the number of participants is yet quite surprising if we consider there are no appropriate shelters and no services. That surprise could some day change into concern and lead to tragedy should there be an overly great number of competitors.
The economic input brought about by such a touristic attraction as those annual races could never be hoped to have some importance without the minimum requirement of building the breakwater previously referred to. Any event of this kind in our area will be doomed to failure and disappearance purely and simply more or less shortly. Mr. Speaker, in eastern Quebec as anywhere else in the country, summer is very short, and the department's efforts to develop tourism, promote with all Quebecers the taste for outdoor life and develop environmental resources will never be qualified as excessive.
The St. Lawrence is a prime ecological resource and the importance of rationally operating that unique stretch of water to the benefit of all citizens in the province without any distinction could never be overemphasized. The development of a recreational harbour in our area would have the immediate effect of extending by at least two months the sailing season on the St. Lawrence and, consequently, allowing more people to enjoy the healthy pleasures provided by a rationally and democratically operated ecological site. The tourist orientation of the Lower St. Lawrence and the Gaspe area was stigmatized on more than one occasion in past years; the host of various reports and studies on this conclude in the same affirmative sense. The positive steps taken by the department to make that important economic activity viable will always be favourably viewed by the whole population.
The trends that are growing each year within the Quebec community will in the next decade give the Department of Tourism increased significance. The higher average purchasing power, the ever stronger appeal of outdoor life and sports, the increase in leisure time will soon turn Quebec into a pivotal table for Canadian and world tourism as long as we take the time to develop properly the strategic tourist sites. Mr. Speaker, no one can deny the obvious attraction the Gaspe Peninsula and the Iles-de-la-Madeleine have for Quebec, Canadian and international tourism, especially since the recent creation of provincial and federal parks, and we do not think it is being bold to say that that trend will increase over the years.
The Anticosti Island recently acquired by the department will only confirm that trend and further stress the need for the strategic development of recreational harbours on the shores of the St. Lawrence above those attraction centres. So it becomes quite obvious that a service city like Rimouski becomes a new neuralgic stop over on the route of sailing tourists when one

recognizes the enormous distances involved in such trips. So we want to point out the urgency of proceedings with the preliminary works and the construction of the breakwater this very year, another step in the progress of this country. So Mr. Speaker, I think it is urgent that the department get on with the job and meet the wish of a very important group in the Rimouski area.
Quebec certainly looks like a late starter in this area, with barely 25 to 30 marinas, compared-I am not saying this out of jealousy-with the more than 2000 which Ontario has, at least 500 of which have been built with the financial assistance of the federal government. I think it would be very wise, if not fair, for the department to do something for the isolated groups who have spent over 10 years trying to obtain the financial backing they need to carry out their marina projects.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the minister who introduced this bill will advise all parties interested in this marina project for the metropolitan city of the Gaspe region and that he will give a favourable reply to this group of Quebec taxpayers. I hope the minister will listen favourably to the wishes of all those who have been seeking for many years the building of a marina in Rimouski. I also hope this bill will make it possible, as I was saying a while ago, for the brave people of the lower St. Lawrence region to benefit from Bill C-7.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate, particularly since Bill C-7 meets, in general philosophical terms, with the approval and has the consent of our party and the opposition generally. Discouraging, however, is the fact that the minister himself is not as keen as we are in advancing this bill through this stage of discussion in the House and he is conspicuous by his absence tonight. This is something we do not greet with as much enthusiasm as we do some provisions in the bill.
We have to be delighted that it is now the intention, as the minister said in his opening remarks, to amalgamate the many sections of departments and agencies which were formerly responsible for small harbours and recreational facilities on lakes, oceans and rivers, which now fall under the purview of the Department of Fisheries and the Environment.
As we know, Mr. Speaker, this was not always so. When one used to apply under this act either for assistance to construct small harbours or facilities on shores, or one attempted to make deals or enter into agreements with individuals, municipalities or provinces, by the time the department acknowledged the request, the responsibility for small harbours had been shifted to some other department. The Department of Transport has several times had responsibility for this particular marine activity. Ministers of Public Works have had responsibility on several occasions, and then sometime in 1973 responsibility was shifted to the Department of Fisheries and the Environment.
June 6, 1977

We are all a little worried over one clause in the bill which provides:
Nothing in this Act applies to or affects
(a)	any harbour, works or property under the jurisdiction of the National Harbours Board or of any harbour Commission established under any Act of Parliament;
We know what the distinction is. These are main port facilities on both coasts which are managed by special commissions or regional agencies. The clause continues:
(b)	any harbour, wharf, pier or breakwater under the control and management of any member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada other than the Minister;-
Now we are getting confused. How many other agencies are still putting their fingers in the pie? Is this really an amalgamation, or will the whole question be referred to other ministers? Are there other jurisdictions? In this regard the bill leaves us in the dark.
Then finally the clause provides:
(c)	Any of the powers or duties of the Minister of Transport or the Minister of Public Works under any other Act of Parliament or regulations made pursuant thereto.
The minister tells us that small recreational and fishing harbours now come under one jurisdiction, and in the same breath he tells us through this bill that the Department of Public Works, the Department of Transport, and a whole series of other departments may also have jurisdiction; that this legislation, which is to be identified as the Fishing and Recreational Harbours Act, may not be under his jurisdiction at all as we move along and try to identify the various parts of the legislation. This leaves me, my colleagues and, I am sure, all Canadians confused as to who has responsibility in this area.
We are also confused over the fact that the minister has identified his new responsibility as having within its jurisdiction at the present time some 2,300 facilities. I would like to point out that 1,500 of those are fishing harbours and 800 are recreational facilities or installations. That does not take into account the hundreds of applications the minister and his department have received to install new facilities in some critical areas on both coasts and in inland water systems as well. What confuses us about this whole business is that we do not find any reference to the minister's new responsibilities in the estimates. He will be spending $35 million this year. That is all we see in the estimates. Having regard to the magnitude of this department and its responsibilities, we find this figure inadequate and not at all in tune with what the minister has identified his responsibilities to be.
Having regard to the most critical nature of this matter on both coasts, one wonders whether there is any way that the minister can address himself to the real need of inland water systems, one of which I will be making particular reference to in my remarks later on. There are many recreational facilities which receive no federal subsidies, and in fact there has been no federal involvement in them at all. We have known these
Fishing and Recreational Harbours facilities to be productive. They generate income in the national and regional interests. One wonders where the government's priorities are. We have to compare the $35 million which was channelled into a most critical area, fisheries, with the money which is spent on Mirabel every year. We saw fit to subsidize the installation at Mirabel by $45 million in one year. No revenue will be generated out of that white elephant. It will take away from some other airdrome which has served us well thus far.
We can also refer to the $500 million which is being put into the CBC every year. Instead of unifying our country and achieving a form of recognition of the difficulties in various regions, we have compounded the misunderstanding with the horrendous bumblings which this institution has perpetrated on Canadians over the last few years.
What about vital industries like fisheries and tourism? Tourism in some provinces is number one. How can we justify spending a mere $35 million? These comparisons have to be made because $35 million is not a very big amount in modern context. What is $35 million in comparison to the Canadian National Railways subsidy of $200 million a year, $500 million to the CBC, and $45 million to Mirabel?
This bill does not offer any comfort to our constituents on the west coast who have recently suffered a phasing out of a transportation subsidy which served 100 communities along the waterways of the west coast. My colleagues and my friends should be able to think back and realize that was a very critical issue in the House of Commons, and still is. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) announced the subsidy and claimed the support of his west coast colleagues on that side of the House. He said that they all had input into this new policy which was called user-pay, and they were serving the best interests of their constituents. One of his friends immediately rectified that by saying he had nothing to do with this monster and wanted to disassociate himself from the minister's comments. That was said in the House publicly. Then there was the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo) who could not master the emotional fitness required to carry out the threat which she issued to the Minister of Transport, namely, that she would resign from the ministry and from the House if this whole question were not reconsidered.
This bill holds out very little comfort to those people. These people will be faced with not being able to go fishing or not being able to take their friends fishing. They will also be faced with a serious situation as to the movement of vital commodities to their shores. I am referring to the small communities on the coast of British Columbia.
I would like to make reference to the situation in my own constituency. In the mid-sixties Williston Lake was created as a result of the construction of the Bennett Dam in central and northern British Columbia. We have a situation now where we have an inland water system which encompasses 680 square miles of water and 1,000 miles of shoreline. There are several native communities which were completely isolated from the mainstream of life by that new water system. These people

June 6, 1977
Fishing and Recreational Harbours used to communicate with the outside world along rivers or roads. Several native communities were totally dislocated and had to be moved when the lake was formed.
It was the wisdom of the department responsible for those particular people to move them close to civilization. When they discovered they could not cope with this new-found society, they moved back into the bush. The type of craft they were using to communicate with the outside world in order to get their mail, bread, butter, salt and sugar, were little canoes and boats. Then they found the little canoes and boats, which they had traditionally used, were no good for this lake which formed, if the wind was right, 20 foot waves. It was an ocean to them. There was no one who offered them any help in acquiring the skills necessary to traverse these waters or in acquiring equipment necessary to traverse these waters. Thus they are totally isolated from the mainstream of life.
The Minister of Transport tells us it is to be user-pay, and if they want to get sugar from across the lake they can buy themselves a $40,000 or a $50,000 ship, hire themselves a crew, and see what they can come up with. At the present time I do not know of any single installation in respect to a harbour, wharf, pier, breakwater, slipway, marina or any part thereof on this lake. There are a number of private installations which would have to be brought in by industry, and they would have their normal access to resources cut off and impaired. They had to adopt a whole new system. They used to be truck loggers, and now they take their logs, pile them on the ice in the winter time and, when the ice melts, the logs sink into the water. They had to buy big ships of an ocean-going type to move their goods and raw materials around this waterway. There was no assistance from anyone. The federal government, the Minister of Transport, and the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) knew they had to buy their own boats. All of a sudden, communities around these lakes were totally isolated, yet no one offered any assistance.
There are other areas in which the Minister of Fisheries should have been involved in this whole mess, as some people call it, in central British Columbia. There were no environmental studies of the sort we talk of now in relation to pipelines and projects such as the James Bay project even though the ministry claims responsibility over several acts, including the legislation designed to protect the environment, notably the Navigable Waters Act. However, from recent inquiries directed to the department I learned that when the minister is asked to make comments or pass judgment, he may express his views with regard to any of these developments such as the Peace River power development, but there is no need for him to issue a licence, and he has no power to hold up such projects if they are discovered to be harmful to the environment. This is critical.
The dam project on the Peace River, as we now know, has changed the temperature in central British Columbia and in some of the northern regions by as much as five degrees. The temperature has moderated to that extend. On the surface one

might think that the people living in the northern areas would greet this change with some enthusiasm. After all, it gets pretty cold up there-40 below in some places. But that is not the whole story. Humidity was also affected. And while we shall not know what the situation really is for another 25 years-officials to whom we have spoken say, "Well, the weather has been bad everywhere; this alteration in the level of humidity will also have repercussions in the region."
I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, what it has done to the farmers. The fact that temperatures are not as cold as they were does not affect them greatly, but it does bother them in the summertime because the humidity detracts from the fast ripening of No. 1 wheat in a region which was a choice area for growing this commodity. Since the lake was created the farmers have yet to raise a decent crop, and many of them are saying that the dam may well be responsible.
Then there are the loggers who, in the middle of November, build their roads into the bush and carry on activities in readiness for their main work which takes place in the winter time. The area is not very accessible in the summer by virtue of its swampy nature. They, too, found there was increased snowfall and insufficient frost in the ground to enable their heavy equipment to be moved in the normal way. They are still improvising and wondering how they will be able to adjust to these new conditions. I am not saying this is all negative. I am pointing out that some of these things were not considered before this project was undertaken, and that the Minister of Fisheries had some responsibility for expressing a judgment with regard to such a massive intervention but failed to take steps to protect the interests of a greater variety of people than those whose interests were considered by the provincial government.
This bill enables the minister to enter into agreements with the provinces and with individuals. I should like to ask him what agreements have been considered with the province of British Columbia in connection with Williston Lake. Certainly, the province is responsible for building this hydro project and I suppose it should have some responsibility for ensuring that the people whose lives have been disturbed, the people who have been isolated, the people whose freedom has been interfered with by this scheme, should at least be given some compensation in the area of transport and so on.
The Findlay River is one of the prime tourist areas in my country. Thousands of people go up that beautiful canyon to find enjoyment and fulfilment during the summer in pursuit of their favourite sport. There are two native communities there. First there is the community of Fort Ware, formerly totally self-sufficient. Today, not only can they not get up the river, because at most times the river is flooded and choked with debris, but they cannot even get access to the lake. They have talked to British Columbia Hydro but there is no comfort there.
The forestry service, which is interested in the lake, has undertaken to do what it can to clear the debris from the waterway but no substantial help is in sight, certainly not from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
June 6, 1977

(Mr. Allmand), who surely should have something to say about the alienation of this particular community and the way in which its traditional rights and lifestyle have been affected.
Then there is the community of Inginika, the one actually displaced by the lake. These people found it impossible to cope with the pressures of the society into which they were moved. They moved back into their old area and are now completely isolated without the equipment or the means of carrying on their old activities. Every year, in the middle of winter as food runs out and fresh vegetables are not obtainable, I find myself making appeals to emergency organizations to fly in vital commodities to keep some of those people alive. Usually it is too late, malnutrition among the children having already taken its toll.
It is absolutely incredible that we should get this kind of document before us without any indication as to the means by which the minister intends to find the money to carry out his mandate. Of course there has been no lack of representation from the people affected by this lake. I have a letter here sent in response to an application originating from a group in Saint John called the River Rats. Further, when program and administrative responsibilities for these harbours were transferred to the Department of Fisheries from the Department of Public Works and the Ministry of Transport in June, 1973, it was done by order in council. When the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications visited the maritimes recently, we read almost every day in the newspapers about some government policy pronouncement concerning this field. The Department of Fisheries claims that the minister suffers because his authority over small craft harbours has been derived from an order in council rather than a legislative enactment. For example, one transport official on the west coast refused to acknowledge the transfer and refused to send his files to fisheries until September, 1976.
The budget of the small craft harbours branch in fisheries is $35 million for the fiscal year 1976/77. Most of the money is used for repair and modernization of the government fishing and recreation wharves on the east and west coasts. There are approximately 2,300 government wharves, with twice as many fishing as recreational wharves, covered by the branch. These facilities are valued at three quarters of a billion dollars.
One of the major criticisms of the bill is the widespread powers being granted to the minister in Clauses 5 and 8. Clause 5 reads:
The Minister may undertake projects for the acquisition, development, construction, improvement or repair of any scheduled harbour or any fishing or recreational harbour to which this Act applies.
Clause 8 reads:
The Minister may, subject to the regulations,
(a)	lease any scheduled harbour or any part thereof to any person;
(b)	grant a licence to any person for the use of any scheduled harbour or any
part thereof; and
(c)	enter into an agreement with the government of any province or any
agency thereof for the occupancy and use of any scheduled harbour or any
part thereof.
According to the branch, Bill C-7 is wide enough for the minister to do it alone or in concert with the provinces and the municipalities. This is especially true in the area of recreation where existing legislation is not clear. Bill C-7 seems to allow the minister to build recreational harbours or wharves wherever he chooses, regardless of provincial or municipal desires, at a time when that party has been advocating greater provincial responsibility and rights. This bill goes against that sentiment. Therefore we urge that it be amended so that the minister will have to work in concert with the provinces.

Under Bill C-7 the government plans to appoint zone managers to look after these government facilities and it plans to institute a licensing program for the use of these facilities. The plan now being discussed would require a fisherman to purchase a licence based on the length of his vessel, $1 per foot. This would be an annual licence and it would allow the fisherman to use any government facility. Fisheries expects
